title: Landing page design for founders past the template
excerpt: Templates fail when the product is specific. Keep the page simple, and replace generic sections with the founder's actual offer, proof, and next step.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree. A simple room for a page that should stay simple once the template is gone.
caption: A short page still needs the real offer in it. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should I abandon the template entirely?
faqs.answer: Keep the simple spine: one opening, a short run of proof, and one action. Replace the placeholder sections with the real offer. A custom layout full of empty columns is the same problem in a new costume.

faqs.question: What do I do if I have no logos or quotes?
faqs.answer: Leave the logo row and the testimonial slider off the page. Describe who the work is for, in your own words. A gray box or an invented quote teaches visitors to doubt the next claim.

faqs.question: When is a template still reasonable?
faqs.answer: When the offer is standard, every sentence has been rewritten, and unused sections are deleted. The failure is publishing the theme's words because the date arrived. Read the page without its cards. The sentences should still explain the product.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The hard part of landing page design for startups arrives when the product stops fitting a template. The page can stay simple. The sections have to become the founder's actual offer: who it is for, what they receive, and what they do next.

A template fails in a specific way. It offers a hero, three feature columns, a logo row, a pricing table, and a testimonial slider whether or not those things exist. Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is blunt about the cost. People often leave in 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is clear early. Generic sections spend that time describing a product the template imagined, not the one you sell.

## What the template got right

Keep the shape. One screen that states the offer. A short run of sections that prove it. One action repeated at the end. That spine is not the problem. Founders outgrow templates because the spine was filled with placeholders: "Feature one," a stock photograph of a laptop, a quote from a person who does not exist, and a price that is not the price.

A simple page is still the right container when the company has one offer. Adding custom illustration, a video background, and a novel navigation does not fix a placeholder. Replacing the placeholder with the real thing does. The craft is in the substitution, section by section.

Hanabi's work on marketing sites follows that idea. Clarity over complexity. The page should feel considered, and it should still be readable in a hurry. A founder who has outgrown a theme does not need a theatrical site. They need the same short page, written and structured around their product.

## Replace each generic section with the real offer

Start with the hero. Delete the template headline and write the offer in the founder's vocabulary. If the product is a narrow tool, say the narrow thing. If the buyer is a specific role, name the role. The template's "Welcome to the future of work" survives in a surprising number of rebrands because nobody assigned the sentence to a person. Assign it.

Replace the three feature columns with the three facts a buyer needs. Those facts are often not features. They might be: what is included, how long it takes to start, and what the team still does by hand. If you only have one fact, use one section. Empty columns are how templates look busy while saying nothing.

Replace the logo row when you do not have logos you may show. A row of gray boxes, or logos from a pilot that ended, teaches the visitor to distrust the next claim. Use a short description of who the work is for instead. Proof can be a concrete project description. It does not have to be a wall of brands.

Replace the pricing table if the price is a conversation. A table of three tiers with invented feature checkmarks pushes people to compare columns you made up. If the commercial step is a call, the section should say what the call is for, how long it is, and what the visitor should bring. If the price is public, then a simple table is honest. Match the section to the way you actually sell.

Replace testimonials you do not have. A fabricated quote is a worse problem than a missing quote. Describe the situation the product is for, in your own words, and move on. When a real customer has said something in public, you can use that sentence and name them. Until then, silence is cleaner.

## Keep the page short on purpose

A specific offer does not require a long page. Specificity is a property of the sentences, not of the scroll depth. One screen of true copy will outlast six screens of template copy because the visitor can finish it and act.

Cut any section that could sit on a competitor's site without a rewrite. "Our values," "Why choose us," and "Our process" are fine only when the content is particular. A four-step process that says Discover, Design, Develop, Deploy is the template speaking. A process that says what the client must bring to the first call, and what they own at the end, is the company speaking.

Images should be of the product, the object, or the people doing the work, cropped so the subject is obvious. Decorative blobs and abstract gradients are the template's way of filling a hole. They do not explain a specific product. If you need a visual and you have no photography yet, show the interface, even as a quiet crop. A real screen is more specific than a generated texture.

Buttons should use the same verb as the offer. If the page is about booking a workshop, the button should say that. Template language like "Learn more" sends people down the page to hunt for the action they already wanted. One verb, used in the hero and again after the proof, is enough.

## When a template is still the right tool

A template remains reasonable when the offer is standard and the words are yours. A local service with one price, one city, and one call to action can wear a theme well if every sentence has been rewritten and the theme's unused sections are deleted. The failure mode is publishing the theme's sentences because the launch date arrived.

Review the page by printing it, or by reading it in a plain text view. If the structure still makes sense without the theme's cards and icons, the content is doing the work. If the page collapses into slogans once the layout is removed, you have reskinned the template. Put the offer back in the sentences before you touch the visual system again.

The same standard applies to a custom design. Custom is not a license to reintroduce three empty columns with better type. Every section still has to survive the question: would this be here if we were not used to seeing it on other sites?

A simple page can still fail to earn the conversation. The difference between a handsome layout and a page that gets the call on the calendar is the next decision: [a pretty homepage versus a page that books calls](/blog/pretty-homepage-versus-booked-calls).
